clue.text: Army unit call intended as a cure

blocks.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps
to dial is to call on the telephone

explanation.surface: A soldier in a unit puts in a sick call, hoping to be treated.
explanation.walkthrough: It is tempting to stop at RE for the Army unit, but the longer abbreviation REME is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Remedial measures are those meant to put something right, like a remedy treating an illness.

clue.text: Used for dressing tots, we hear

definitions.note: describes the tool by its use rather than naming a noun

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling of the word that tots up is not what counts

blocks.note: to tot up is to add up figures

explanation.surface: Someone is putting clothes on small children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' suggests clothing and 'tots' toddlers; in fact dressing timber means shaping it, and tots are sums.
explanation.definitionFit: An adze is an arched axe-like tool carpenters use for trimming and shaping rough timber.

clue.text: Part of cooker provided on drawing capital?

blocks.note: the hob is the top of a cooker where pans sit
drawing is a form of art

explanation.surface: Someone is sketching a cooker part, wondering if that is a good asset.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that this is a state capital, not a national one: Hobart is the capital of Tasmania.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobart is the chief city and seat of government of the Australian island state of Tasmania.

clue.text: Writer likes New York gravity, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the preceding letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
NY is the standard abbreviation for New York
g is the physics symbol for acceleration due to gravity

explanation.surface: An author enjoys the seriousness of New York.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Kingsley was the Victorian novelist whose works appear at 13 and 20/22 in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley was a nineteenth-century English clergyman and novelist, so he is an author.

clue.text: Dangerous post

blocks.note: surface reading: a risky job or position
setter's reading: an item of mail that can explode

explanation.walkthrough: Post looks like a job, as in a dangerous posting abroad; here it is mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a device is an explosive concealed in an envelope or parcel and sent through the mail.

clue.text: Follower of flickering torch needing to take in oxygen

indicators.note: a flickering flame is unsteady, so the letters of the torch move about
taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A torch flame is guttering and needs more oxygen to keep going.
explanation.definitionFit: A cohort can mean a supporter or companion, especially in American usage, so it fits follower.

clue.text: Unfeeling comment - no good, completely useless

indicators.note: no good tells you to drop the abbreviation for good from the word for comment

blocks.note: a dead limb has no feeling
a gloss is an explanatory comment on a text

explanation.surface: A cold remark is dismissed as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: G is the usual abbreviation for good, so it is removed from GLOSS.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead loss is a person or thing that is wholly worthless or a total failure.

clue.text: Smart one with the cones

blocks.note: first meaning: neat and trim in appearance
second meaning: a conifer bearing cones

explanation.surface: A sharply dressed person is in charge of the traffic cones.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means neat and well turned out, and is also an evergreen conifer that bears cones.

clue.text: Cold compartment used for a buffet outside church

blocks.note: a means one, and I is the Roman numeral one
CE is the Church of England
to buffet or box someone is to strike them

explanation.surface: A chilled section is set aside for a buffet meal held outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Buffet looks like a meal but is the verb to strike; 'outside' places it beyond church.
explanation.definitionFit: An icebox is a chamber or compartment kept cold, especially the freezer section of a refrigerator.

clue.text: Could be a pet tip, say

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the word for tip is matched by its sound

blocks.note: a peak is a tip or summit

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a tip that might suit a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pekingese, a small long-haired toy dog, is a common pet, hence 'could be' for an example.

clue.text: The sailor's asking for an annulment

blocks.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman; 's here means 'is'
rogation is a solemn asking or supplication, as in Rogation Days

explanation.surface: A sailor is requesting that a marriage or contract be cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: Rogation, from Latin rogare 'to ask', survives in the church's Rogation Days of prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrogation is the formal repeal or cancelling of a law or agreement, the same as annulment.

clue.text: One's stupid to make it dull around the west

indicators.note: around says the pair of words sit either side of the compass point

blocks.note: dim means dull, not bright
W is the abbreviation for west
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is slow-witted enough to tone down a scene around the west.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words 'it' and 'dull' go round W, with dull first.
explanation.definitionFit: A dimwit is a slow, foolish person; 'one's stupid' describes such a person.

clue.text: 4's work

blocks.note: surface reading: something done by the answer at 4
setter's reading: a novel written by that author

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the writer at 4; this is his 1855 Elizabethan seafaring adventure.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1855 novel of Elizabethan adventure at sea was written by Charles Kingsley, so it is his work.

clue.text: The speed of a star with no centre

indicators.note: having no centre means the single middle letter is taken out

blocks.note: a star is a famous person

explanation.surface: A star has lost its core and a physicist asks how fast it moves.
explanation.walkthrough: CELEBRITY has nine letters, so its centre is the fifth, B.
explanation.definitionFit: Celerity is a formal word for swiftness or rapidity of motion.

clue.text: Rascal upset the seaman

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rogue has annoyed a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A lascar was a sailor from India or Southeast Asia serving on European ships.

clue.text: Flair shown in sitar playing attempt

indicators.note: playing suggests the instrument's name being played about with and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: A musician's first go at the sitar shows real talent.
explanation.definitionFit: Artistry is creative skill or talent, which is what flair means here.

clue.text: Wormy bit of deal needing treatment? Oh, I say!

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is its opening letter only
treatment works material over, so these letters are processed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of deal

explanation.surface: Woodworm-ridden timber needs treating, prompting a cry of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal is pine timber, which fits the wormy wood of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated exclamations of surprise or mild shock, interchangeable in speech.

clue.text: By which one can alter handle

definitions.text: By which one can alter handle

blocks.clueFragment: By which one can alter handle
blocks.note: surface reading: a tool for changing a door or cup handle

blocks.clueFragment: By which one can alter handle
blocks.note: setter's reading: handle is slang for a name, changed by a legal document

explanation.walkthrough: Handle is informal for a person's name; in Britain one changes it formally by a legal deed.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the legal document by which a person in the UK formally changes their name.

clue.text: Breaking of the law, say, concerning gun part

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the word for a breaking of the law counts by its sound

blocks.note: a breach is an infringement of a law

explanation.surface: A legal infringement involving part of a firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: The breech is the rear part of a gun barrel where the cartridge is loaded.

clue.text: 4's work

blocks.note: surface reading: something done by the answer at 4
setter's reading: a children's book written by that author

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the writer at 4; this is his 1863 fairy tale about a chimney sweep's boy.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1863 children's fantasy about Tom the chimney sweep was written by Charles Kingsley.

clue.text: Worker in Kent, one getting grain?

blocks.note: first meaning: a hop picker; Kent, a county in south-east England, was famous for hop fields
second meaning: a funnel-shaped container into which grain is fed

explanation.surface: A farm labourer in Kent collects the harvest.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a seasonal hop picker and also a feed container that receives grain for a mill.

clue.text: See 20
To drill can be tedious

blocks.note: first meaning: making a hole, as a verb form
second meaning: dull and wearisome

explanation.surface: A complaint that repetitive military drill is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Drill suggests army practice, which fits 'tedious'; here it means making holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a hole with a drill is the act of piercing, and a tedious thing fails to hold interest.

clue.text: Put on society clothing, or track suit?

blocks.note: to sport something is to wear it showily
S is an abbreviation for society
wear means clothing, as in evening wear

explanation.surface: A shopper wonders whether to dress up for society or wear a tracksuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the tracksuit as one example of the category.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracksuit is an example of garments designed for athletic activity.

clue.text: Preoccupied sailor has turn round piano

indicators.note: a turn sends the word for sailor back the other way
round says the sailor's letters encircle the musical abbreviation

blocks.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
p is the musical marking for piano, soft

explanation.surface: A distracted sailor takes a turn at the piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapt means wholly absorbed or engrossed, so someone rapt is lost in thought.

clue.text: Old city set up beside a stone

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia
by means beside

explanation.surface: An ancient city has been built next to a stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruby is a precious red gemstone, so it is a stone in the jeweller's sense.

clue.text: Name the number below

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name
a number is something that numbs, and ether is an anaesthetic

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to state the figure written underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: Number is read as 'numb-er', a thing that makes you numb: the anaesthetic ether.
explanation.definitionFit: Nether is an adjective meaning lower or under, as in the nether regions.

clue.text: Account after writing information sheet

blocks.note: hand means handwriting
a bill is an account of money owed

explanation.surface: A bill follows the writing of a leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the account second, following the writing.
explanation.definitionFit: A handbill is a printed leaflet distributed by hand to give notice or advertise.
